items.title: Qwen3-Coder parser: lazy tool-call trigger never fires when model skips both <tool_call> and <function=
items.body:
## Summary

The Qwen3-Coder chat parser (`common_chat_params_init_qwen3_coder`, added in #26252) has a documented workaround for models that omit the opening `<tool_call>` wrapper while still emitting `<function=name>`. In practice the model can deviate further than that, abandoning the structured format entirely, and the lazy grammar trigger never fires, so the response falls through as plain content instead of `tool_calls`.

## Root cause

The trigger that switches into constrained decoding only watches for a literal `<tool_call>` or `<function=` substring in the raw output stream:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c/common/chat.cpp#L1241

```cpp
(reasoning << p.content(p.until_one_of({ "<tool_call>", "<function=" })) << tool_calls);
```

The existing workaround, one line above, acknowledges partial omission:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c/common/chat.cpp#L1232

```cpp
// Qwen3-Coder models may occasionally omit the <tool_call> token.
```

...and makes the *first* call's `<tool_call>\n` wrapper optional in the grammar. That only helps if the model still emits `<function=`. When it emits neither trigger string at all, `p.content()` consumes the whole response as free text and the tool-call branch is never entered.

Auto-detection for this parser (matched by the chat template containing `<tool_call>`, `<function=`, `<parameter=`):

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c/common/chat.cpp#L3182-L3186

## Repro

- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Q8_0
- Build: a local rebase/merge commit (b10361) on top of #26252 (f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c, merged 2026-08-02, that commit is linked above for the source references since the local merge commit itself was never pushed and has no public ref; confirmed the referenced lines are unchanged between the two, this is not a missing-fix situation, the specialized parser is active)
- Chat template: Jinja template instructing `<tool_call>\n<function=name>\n<parameter=...>` (matches the auto-detect heuristic above)
- `tool_choice`: unset/auto, any temperature
- Real production output, verbatim, no `tool_calls` in the response, `finish_reason: stop`:

```
I'll check your cron jobs to find the daily briefing one and trigger it.

[cron(action='list')]
```

The model had a real tool available (name `cronjob`, note it also got the name wrong) but never entered tool-call grammar at all; the response was delivered as ordinary assistant text.

## Why this isn't just a bad prompt

Confirmed deterministic and prompt-dependent, not sampling noise: replaying the exact same request at `temperature=0` reproduces this exact fabricated output 5/5 times, byte-for-byte identical. The same request at default temperature produces a correct `tool_calls` response 5/5 times. Same template, same tool schema, same model, only the sampled decoding path differs, and greedy decoding happens to land on a path that never emits either trigger string for this particular prompt.

## Suggested direction

Broaden the "did the model intend a tool call" signal beyond exact-match on `<tool_call>`/`<function=`, e.g. a lower-confidence secondary trigger on tool-name-shaped call syntax in free text, or, if that's out of scope, a docs note that the existing omission workaround doesn't cover the model abandoning the format entirely would at least set expectations correctly.

items.title: Eval bug: gemma4 peg template intermittently unparseable with long multi-line tool-call string arguments
items.body:
## Summary

Native tool calling with the `peg-gemma4` chat template intermittently
produces unparseable output when a tool call must carry long multi-line
string arguments (source code with quotes, newlines, and digest strings).
Short-argument calls (single paths, small queries) are reliable in the same
sessions. Failures surface server-side as
`common_chat_peg_parse: unparsed peg-gemma4 output: …` followed by an
unusable response body.

## Environment

- llama.cpp builds `14d3ba4` and `b10078` (both reproduce)
- Model: Gemma 4 26B-A4B instruction-tuned, QAT, UD-Q4_K_XL GGUF
- macOS / Metal, `--jinja`, native tool calling, `--parallel 1`
- Speculative decoding via `--spec-type draft-mtp` (an MTP draft head);
  failures also reproduce with speculation disabled
- Sampling: temp 0.2, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, repeat-penalty 1.0

## Observations

1. Repro: seed a workspace with a small `calc.py` + `test_calc.py`; request
   an edit that requires sending replacement file content as a tool-call
   string argument. First read-only calls parse fine; the edit call fails
   intermittently (most attempts in our runs).
2. Failure content shows two modes: (a) degenerate repetition of tool-call
   blocks or of a short token sequence, accelerated to ~99% draft
   acceptance by MTP; (b) malformed special-token quoting inside the
   argument payload (`<|"|>`-delimited strings interrupted by content).
3. Raising repetition penalties makes things worse: penalized sampling
   corrupted a verbatim tool name by one character in our logs
   (`…_3c6d768552ba` → `…_3d6d768552ba`), so format fidelity requires
   penalty-free sampling.
4. Enabling native thinking (`--reasoning-budget`) increases failure
   frequency; disabling it does not eliminate failures.

## Ask

- Whether the peg-gemma4 grammar can constrain string interiors (or recover
  from stray bytes) rather than rejecting the entire generation.
- Whether draft acceptance should be dampened when the accepted window is
  self-similar (anti-loop guard under speculative decoding).

Happy to provide full event-log excerpts and server-log signatures on request.

items.title: Eval bug: named/required tool_choice not enforced for Qwen3.6 templates when enable_thinking=false
items.body:
### Name and Version

Reproduced identically on three builds (CPU-only, `cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`, Linux x86_64):
- `f280b26983` (current at time of testing)
- `4d19b28` (master, includes #27679)
- `60addddf3c` (about a week older)

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-APEX-I-Compact.gguf --jinja -c 4096 --port 18081

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18081/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France? One word."}],
  "chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking":false},
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"assist","description":"web research","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"query":{"type":"string"}},"required":["query"]}}}],
  "tool_choice":"required","temperature":0,"max_tokens":600}'
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With a Qwen3-family chat template (Qwen3.5/3.6 MoE, embedded GGUF template, handled by the auto-parser path) and `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}`, the `tool_choice: "required"` constraint (and likewise a named function `tool_choice`) is **not enforced**: the model free-runs plain prose until `max_tokens` (`finish_reason: "length"`), returns no `tool_calls`, and `content` stays empty when the run ends inside what the parser treats as reasoning.

Control experiments on the same build and GGUF, changing exactly one variable each:

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| same request, thinking **enabled** (omit the kwarg) | tool call correctly forced ✓ |
| same request, **Gemma-3-family** GGUF/template | tool call correctly forced ✓ |
| same schema via `response_format: json_schema` instead of tools | grammar correctly enforced ✓ |
| `tool_choice: "auto"` | behaves as expected (model may answer) ✓ |

So the grammar machinery itself is fine — the combination *Qwen3 template + `enable_thinking: false` + forced tool choice* is what loses the constraint. `stop` sequences are unrelated (reproduced with and without).

At temperature 0 the failure is fully deterministic. Practical impact: OpenAI-compatible agent frameworks that force the selected tool via named `tool_choice` (to generate its arguments) silently break on these very common Qwen3 no-think setups — the doomed generation runs to the token cap on every decision.

Happy to provide full server logs or test other template families if useful.

*Disclosure: this report was prepared with AI assistance (Claude); the bisection across the three builds and all control experiments were run and verified by hand on real hardware.*

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

```shell
"choices":[{"finish_reason":"length","message":{"role":"assistant","content":"", "reasoning_content":"Thinking Process:\n\n1. **Identify the us…"}}]
(with enable_thinking:false the free-run lands in content instead; no tool_calls either way)
```

items.title: Misc. bug: llama-server tool-calling grammar crashes with "Unexpected empty grammar stack" depending only on parameter description text
items.body:
### Name and Version

$./llama-server --version
version: 0.2.0-dev (build 10587, commit 3f545becc)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
GGML_CUDA_ENABLE_UNIFIED_MEMORY=1 \
~/Code/llama.cpp/build-hip/bin/llama-server \
  -m /srv/hermes/ai/models/gguf/qwen/qwen3-coder-30b-a3b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf \
  --load-mode dio \
  -ngl 999 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8083 \
  --alias hermes-coder \
  --jinja \
  -c 16384 \
  -np 1 \
  --reasoning off \
  --reasoning-budget 0
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I found a reproducible tool-calling grammar failure in llama-server.

The failure can be triggered by changing only the natural-language description
of an optional string property in a tool's JSON Schema.

The structure of the JSON Schema remains unchanged.

I originally encountered this while using OpenCode with Qwen3-Coder, but I was
able to reproduce the issue directly against llama-server's
/v1/chat/completions endpoint, without OpenCode or LiteLLM.

The request contains one tool named glob with:

pattern: required string
path: optional string
tool_choice: auto

The user prompt is:

```text
Use glob exactly once to find TypeScript files under src/.

After the tool returns, respond with only the first 3 file paths.
Do not use any other tool.
```

I have attached two otherwise identical requests:

working.json
failing.json

They differ in only one string.

Working description
The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null".

Request:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @working.json | jq
```
This succeeds and returns a valid tool call similar to:
```json
{
  "finish_reason": "tool_calls",
  "message": {
    "tool_calls": [
      {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
          "name": "glob",
          "arguments": "{\"pattern\":\"src/**/*.ts\"}"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
Failing description

The only change is adding:

```text
- simply omit it for the default behavior.
```
The full failing description is:

The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior.

Request:
```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @failing.json | jq
```
This fails with HTTP 500:
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": 500,
    "message": "got exception: Unexpected empty grammar stack after accepting piece: ? (30)",
    "type": "server_error"
  }
}
```
Additional isolation

I tested the suspicious fragments separately.

All of these work:
```text
DO NOT enter "undefined".
DO NOT enter "null".
DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null".
```
The failure appears when this additional phrase is present:
```text
- simply omit it for the default behavior.
```
In an earlier failing run, instead of immediately returning HTTP 500, the tool
arguments started degenerating into question marks:
```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "glob",
    "arguments": "{\"pattern\":\"????????????????????????????????????????????????????"
  }
}
```
The server then reported the grammar exception.

Expected behavior

Changing natural-language text inside a JSON Schema description can reasonably
change what the model attempts to generate, but it should not cause the grammar
or constrained-decoding state to become invalid and abort the request with an
HTTP 500.

If the model attempts to generate arguments that do not satisfy the grammar, I
would expect the grammar implementation to constrain or reject those tokens
without reaching an invalid empty-stack state.

Actual behavior

llama-server throws:
```text
Unexpected empty grammar stack after accepting piece: ? (30)
```
and aborts the request.

### Important note about reproducibility

After reducing the request, I found that the failure is not deterministic.

The same request can produce different outcomes across runs.

Therefore, I no longer think that the parameter description itself deterministically causes the grammar failure.

Instead, the description appears to affect the model's generated token path.
Some generated paths can eventually expose the grammar failure.

My concern is therefore primarily about grammar robustness:

even if the model generates malformed or unexpected output, accepting a token
should not leave the grammar in an invalid empty-stack state and abort the
request with HTTP 500.

Thanks!

[working.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31352301/working.json)
[failing.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31352302/failing.json)

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
slot      iterate: id  0 | task 766 | got exception: Unexpected empty grammar stack after accepting piece: ? (30)
srv    send_error: task id = 766, error: got exception: Unexpected empty grammar stack after accepting piece: ? (30)
slot      release: id  0 | task 766 | stop processing: n_tokens = 513, truncated = 0
srv          stop: cancel task, id_task = 766
```
</details>

items.title: server: tool_choice: "required" accepted but not enforced on templates with supports_preserve_reasoning=true
items.body:
# `tool_choice: "required"` is accepted but not enforced on templates with `supports_preserve_reasoning: true`

### Name and Version

```
build_info: b330-84e908c62
```
Built locally for CUDA 13.0, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121 -DCMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS="-O2"`.

### Operating systems

Linux (aarch64, NVIDIA GB10 / sm_121)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

`llama-server`, and the chat/grammar layer under `common/` (`chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp`).

### Command line

```
llama-server -m qwen36-NVFP4-MTP-HQ.gguf --host 0.0.0.0 --port 11435 \
  -c 131072 --jinja -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type draft-mtp
```

### Problem description

`llama-server` accepts `"tool_choice": "required"` on `/v1/chat/completions` without error or
warning, and then does not enforce it, on models whose chat template llama.cpp classifies with
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`.

Instead of being constrained to emit a tool call, the model generates freely until `max_tokens`
is exhausted. The request returns `finish_reason: "length"` with `predicted_n` equal to the full
budget and no `tool_calls`. In the runs I inspected the tail of the output had degenerated into a
repeating emoji sequence, which is consistent with generation being unconstrained rather than
grammar-limited.

The failure is **silent and expensive**: a caller that relies on `required` for structured output
receives ordinary prose, no error, and pays the maximum token cost of the request every time.

Two servers on the same host, same binary, same build string, both `--jinja`, differ only in the
model/template:

| | fast lane | smart lane |
|---|---|---|
| model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (NVFP4, MTP) | Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) |
| `supports_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_parallel_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_object_arguments` | true | true |
| **`supports_preserve_reasoning`** | **true** | **false** |
| `tool_choice: "required"` | **ignored** | honoured |

`supports_preserve_reasoning` is the only differing capability in `/props → chat_template_caps`.

**On reproducing this without my exact file:** the GGUF above is a local conversion and is not
something you can download, so please do not treat the filename as the repro target. The trigger
appears to be the *chat template* — specifically whichever templates llama.cpp classifies
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`, i.e. a `<think>`-style reasoning template. Any model whose
`/props → chat_template_caps` reports that flag together with `supports_tool_calls: true` should
show it. `repro.sh` prints both flags up front so it is obvious at a glance whether a given server
is a candidate. I am happy to attach the exact template text if that helps.

### What is NOT the cause (ruled out by measurement)

- **The model.** An identical hand-written GBNF grammar posted to `/completion` forces a perfect
  tool call on both servers, from a prompt with no intent to call anything. Section B of the
  reproducer is this control.
- **Grammar sampling generally.** `root ::= "BANANA"` is honoured on the affected server.
- **Speculative decoding.** The control above succeeds with `--spec-type draft-mtp` active.
- **Reasoning parsing.** Sending `"reasoning_format": "none"` does not change the behaviour.
- **Token budget.** Identical failure at `max_tokens` 500 / 1500 / 3000 / 5000 — all fully
  consumed, `reasoning_content` exactly 801 chars each time.
- **The tool-call syntax.** Both templates emit `<tool_call>…</tool_call>` with `<|im_start|>`.

### Why this looks like a defect rather than unsupported behaviour

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp` appears to intend enforcement on this path:

```cpp
// ~line 84
bool include_grammar = has_response_format || (has_tools &&
        ((inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO && !trigger_marker.empty()) ||
          inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_REQUIRED));

// ~line 89 — REQUIRED yields a NON-lazy (eager) grammar
data.grammar_lazy = !has_response_format && inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO;

// ~line 369 and ~line 500 — for REQUIRED the tool calls are NOT made optional
if (!require_calls) { tool_calls = p.optional(tool_calls); }
```

So a grammar is built, marked eager, and tool calls are non-optional — yet generation is
evidently unconstrained. I have not isolated the specific line where enforcement is lost; that
likely needs a debug build dumping the emitted GBNF for the two templates.

### Steps to Reproduce

Full script at the bottom of this issue. `./repro.sh <host:port>` exits **1** when the bug reproduces and **0**
when `required` is honoured — it was verified to discriminate between the two servers above.

```bash
curl -s http://HOST:PORT/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello, how are you today?"}],
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_disk_free",
    "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"host":{"type":"string"}},"required":["host"]}}}],
  "tool_choice":"required","max_tokens":2000,"temperature":0}'
```

Expected: a `tool_calls` response. Actual on an affected template: `finish_reason: "length"`,
`predicted_n` == `max_tokens`, no `tool_calls`.

### Relevant log output

```
finish_reason : length
predicted_n   : 2000
tool_calls    : NONE
content tail  : '🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️…'

# control, same server, hand-written grammar via /completion:
'<tool_call>{"name": "get_disk_free", "arguments": {"host": "beta"}}</tool_call>'
```


### Possibly related open issues

- **#26781** — *"enable_thinking forced true in jinja/caps.cpp capability probe leaks into
  non-DeepSeek templates"*. Same model family (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), same subsystem, and a very
  similar end state: budget consumed inside `reasoning_content`, no `tool_calls`, a silent dead
  end for an API consumer. **Differences:** that report needs ~38-41 turns of accumulated context
  and ends `finish_reason: "stop"`; this one reproduces on a **single turn** and ends
  `finish_reason: "length"`, and it is specific to `tool_choice: "required"`, which that issue does
  not mention. Worth noting that my build **contains** the first-bad-commit bisected there
  (`0ef6e55e`, #26398 — verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor`). If these share a root cause,
  the single-turn reproducer here may be the cheaper way to bisect it; happy to be closed as a
  duplicate if a maintainer sees them as the same defect.
- **#26530** — Qwen3-Coder template failing to emit `<tool_call>` with large prompts and many
  tools. Different trigger (prompt size, `auto` rather than `required`) but the same "template
  fails to produce a tool call" family.

### Separate, smaller issue found alongside

The OpenAI named-function form of `tool_choice` is rejected by type and silently downgraded to
the default on **both** servers:

```
W Wrong type supplied for parameter 'tool_choice'. Expected 'string',
  using default value: [json.exception.type_error.302] type must be string, but is object
```

`{"type":"function","function":{"name":"X"}}` is the documented OpenAI shape. Callers sending it
get `auto` behaviour with only a server-side log line. Worth either supporting the object form or
returning a 400 rather than silently changing the semantics of the request.


### `repro.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Minimal reproducer: tool_choice:"required" is accepted but not enforced
# on a chat template that llama.cpp classifies supports_preserve_reasoning=true.
#
# Usage: ./repro.sh <host:port>            e.g. ./repro.sh localhost:8080
# Exit 0 = required was honoured (no bug). Exit 1 = accepted-but-ignored (bug reproduced).
set -u
EP="${1:?usage: repro.sh <host:port>}"

TOOLS='[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_disk_free",
  "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"host":{"type":"string"}},"required":["host"]}}}]'
# A prompt the model has no reason to answer with a tool call. That is the point:
# tool_choice:"required" is supposed to compel one anyway.
MSG='[{"role":"user","content":"Hello, how are you today?"}]'

echo "== server =="
curl -s "http://$EP/props" | python3 -c "
import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin)
print('  model :', (d.get('model_path') or '?').split('/')[-1])
print('  build :', d.get('build_info'))
caps=d.get('chat_template_caps',{})
print('  supports_tool_calls        :', caps.get('supports_tool_calls'))
print('  supports_preserve_reasoning:', caps.get('supports_preserve_reasoning'))
"

echo
echo "== A. tool_choice:\"required\" (EXPECTED: a tool call) =="
RESP=$(curl -s "http://$EP/v1/chat/completions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"local\",\"messages\":$MSG,\"tools\":$TOOLS,\"tool_choice\":\"required\",\"max_tokens\":2000,\"temperature\":0}")
echo "$RESP" | python3 -c "
import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); c=d['choices'][0]; m=c['message']
tc=m.get('tool_calls')
print('  finish_reason :', c.get('finish_reason'))
print('  predicted_n   :', d.get('timings',{}).get('predicted_n'))
print('  tool_calls    :', tc[0]['function']['name'] if tc else 'NONE  <-- not enforced')
print('  content tail  :', repr((m.get('content') or '')[-80:]))
"
HAS_CALL=$(echo "$RESP" | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(1 if (json.load(sys.stdin)['choices'][0]['message'].get('tool_calls')) else 0)")

echo
echo "== B. CONTROL: same model, hand-written GBNF via /completion =="
echo "   (proves the model CAN be grammar-forced against its intent)"
curl -s "http://$EP/completion" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
 "prompt":"User asks: hello how are you?\nAssistant:",
 "grammar":"root ::= \"<tool_call>{\\\"name\\\": \\\"get_disk_free\\\", \\\"arguments\\\": {\\\"host\\\": \\\"\" host \"\\\"}}</tool_call>\"\nhost ::= \"alpha\" | \"beta\"",
 "n_predict":80,"temperature":0}' | python3 -c "
import json,sys; print('  output:', repr((json.load(sys.stdin).get('content') or '').strip())[:100])
"

echo
if [ "$HAS_CALL" = "1" ]; then
  echo "RESULT: required WAS honoured — bug not reproduced on this server."; exit 0
else
  echo "RESULT: BUG REPRODUCED — tool_choice:\"required\" accepted without error, no tool call,"
  echo "        full token budget consumed, while the control proves grammar forcing works."
  exit 1
fi
```

items.title: Qwen3 TAG_WITH_TAGGED tool format: p.json() fails on array<object> parameter values; partial tool_call leaked to client poisons multi-turn history

labels.name: regression
labels.description: A regression introduced in a new build (something that was previously working correctly)

labels.name: chat parser
labels.description: Issues related to the chat parser and chat templates

items.body:
## Summary

When a tool has a parameter whose JSON schema is `array<object>` (e.g. `[{"type":"web"}]`) and the model (Qwen3 family using the `TAG_WITH_TAGGED` / `<tool_call><function=...><parameter=...>` format) emits it as the inner value of a `<parameter>` tag, the autoparser's PEG `p.json()` fails mid-stream. Two cascading problems follow:

1. **Root parse failure.** `build_tool_parser_tag_tagged` uses `p.json()` for any parameter that doesn't resolve to a string schema. On array-of-object values the PEG parser aborts, the request ends in a 500 with `Failed to parse input at pos N: <tool_call>...`.
2. **Partial state leaked to the client.** Before the failure, the partial-parse fallback at `common/chat.cpp:2158` returns whatever AST was built so far. For streaming (`is_partial=true`) this surfaces to the client as an SSE delta containing `tool_calls[0].function.arguments = "{"` (one character). The client, acting correctly per the OpenAI spec, appends this tool_call to conversation history.
3. **History poisoning.** Every subsequent request replays that history. `func_args_not_string` at `common/chat.cpp:1842-1860` eagerly parses `tool_calls[].function.arguments` as JSON and throws a 500 on the bare `{`, so the conversation is now stuck: every follow-up crashes with `Failed to parse tool call arguments as JSON: ... unexpected end of input`, even though the client did nothing wrong.

Net effect: a single tool-call attempt with a complex parameter permanently wedges the conversation until the client manually strips the assistant message from history.

## Name and Version

```
version: 8759 (2b2cd57de)
built with GNU 11.4.0 for Linux x86_64
```

HEAD of master as of 2026-04-11, i.e. PR #21216 is included (verified commit `26229755c` is in the binary).

## Operating systems

Linux

## GGML backends

CUDA

## Hardware

4x RTX 3090

## Models

`Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-Q4_K_M` (GGUF). The bug is not specific to this model — it reproduces with any model whose template routes to `TAG_WITH_TAGGED` tool format.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Launch the server with jinja enabled and any tool set containing an `array<object>` parameter:
   ```
   llama-server -m Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 163840 -fa on \
                --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --jinja
   ```
2. Send a chat completion with a tool definition like:
   ```json
   {
     "type": "function",
     "function": {
       "name": "firecrawl_search",
       "parameters": {
         "type": "object",
         "properties": {
           "query":   {"type": "string"},
           "limit":   {"type": "integer"},
           "sources": {
             "type": "array",
             "items": {
               "type": "object",
               "properties": {"type": {"type": "string", "enum": ["web","images","news"]}},
               "required": ["type"]
             }
           }
         },
         "required": ["query"]
       }
     }
   }
   ```
   and a user prompt that naturally requires calling it with `sources` set.
3. The model emits (captured via a request-dumping proxy in front of llama-server):
   ```
   <tool_call>
   <function=firecrawl_search>
   <parameter=limit>
   10
   </parameter>
   <parameter=query>
   pop culture trends USA March April 2026 movies music TV shows celebrities
   </parameter>
   <parameter=sources>
   [{"type": "web"},
   ```
4. Server responds with 500 in the SSE stream:
   ```
   Failed to parse input at pos 518: <tool_call>
   <function=firecrawl_search>
   ...
   <parameter=sources>
   [{"type": "web"},
   ```
5. Inspection of the SSE stream of that same request shows a **preceding** delta event:
   ```json
   {"choices":[{"delta":{"tool_calls":[{"index":0,"id":"...",
     "type":"function","function":{"name":"firecrawl_search","arguments":"{"}}]}}]}
   ```
   i.e. `arguments = "{"` (one character) was already pushed to the client before the stream fails.
6. Any follow-up chat completion that replays the assistant message as conversation history now fails with:
   ```
   Failed to parse tool call arguments as JSON:
   [json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 1, column 2:
   syntax error while parsing object key - unexpected end of input; expected string literal
   ```

## Root cause (pointers)

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp` around line 367 in `build_tool_parser_tag_tagged`:

```cpp
(schema_info.resolves_to_string(param_schema) ?
    p.tool_arg_string_value(p.schema(until_suffix, ..., param_schema, true)) :
    p.tool_arg_json_value(p.schema(p.json(), ..., param_schema, false)) + p.space())
```

For non-string parameters the generated rule calls `p.json()`, which appears to be unable to parse JSON whose value is `array<object>` inside a `<parameter>` tag context. Possibly related: nested-object backtracking, or lookahead for the closing `</parameter>` interfering with the JSON grammar. I have not pinned the exact failure site inside `p.json()` yet — happy to dig further if useful.

The partial-parse fallback at `common/chat.cpp:2158-2178` is what surfaces `"{"` to the client during streaming, and `func_args_not_string` at `common/chat.cpp:1842-1860` is the secondary crash point that poisons the conversation.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Parser:** Either fix `p.json()` to parse arbitrary nested JSON inside `<parameter>` tag context, or (simpler) switch the non-string branch to use `until_suffix`-based capture + a post-parse `json::parse` on the raw slice. The latter matches how many real-world clients emit structured parameter values and avoids coupling grammar with schema.
2. **Streaming safety:** `is_partial` should not emit a `tool_calls[].function.arguments` delta unless the accumulated content is at least a syntactically valid JSON *prefix* that the client can safely append to (or, simplest, flush only when the full tool_call is complete). Emitting `"{"` and then aborting is strictly worse than emitting nothing.
3. **Replay tolerance:** `func_args_not_string` should not throw a 500 when a prior `tool_calls[].function.arguments` in the input history is not valid JSON. It can either leave the string as-is (letting the template render it verbatim) or wrap it for the template. Throwing forces the client to clean up after the server's own broken output.

## Notes

Not a duplicate of #20867 (that one was about `MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD`, fixed by #21216, which is already in this build).

When using a thinking model (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) as a backend for **GitHub Copilot Chat in Agent mode** (VS Code), the server returns a 500 error `Failed to parse input at pos N` during multi-turn agentic tool-calling workflows.

```bash
llama-server \
  -hf unsloth/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q8_0 \
  --jinja \
  --reasoning-format deepseek \
  -lv 4 \
  --log-timestamps \
  --log-file ./llamaLog.txt
```

The llama-server is configured as an OpenAI-compatible backend for VS Code's GitHub Copilot Chat Agent mode. In this workflow:

1. Copilot sends a chat completion request with many tools (`read_file`, `grep_search`, `semantic_search`, `list_dir`, `memory`, etc.)
2. The model thinks inside `<think>...</think>`, then calls a tool via `<tool_call>...</tool_call>`
3. The tool result is returned to the model, which thinks again and calls more tools
4. This multi-step loop continues until the model produces a final answer

During these multi-turn interactions, the model frequently outputs a short natural language transition sentence between `</think>` and `<tool_call>`, such as:
- `让我再查看一些额外的信息来完善分析。` ("Let me check some more information to refine the analysis.")
- `让我继续查看更多关键文件来完善分析。` ("Let me continue reviewing more key files.")

The lazy grammar trigger correctly identifies `<tool_call>` and constrains the generation from that point onward (the tool call XML is well-formed). However, when the **post-generation PEG parser** (`Parsing PEG input with format peg-native`) tries to parse the complete model output, it receives the **entire output** including the prefix text before `<tool_call>`. Since the grammar's `root ::= tool-call` expects the input to start with `<tool_call>`, any prefix text causes a parse failure. This breaks the entire agentic loop.

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Problem description
When a remote MCP server returns a tool result where the real data lives in
`structuredContent` and `content` is an empty array (a valid shape per the MCP
spec — some servers omit the duplicate serialized-JSON TextContent block),
the WebUI's MCP tool-call panel shows "No output" and the model receives
nothing, even though the HTTP response is 200 OK and contains full data.

Verified independently with curl against the same MCP server, same token:
the server returns something shaped like:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "content": [],
    "structuredContent": {
      "accounts": [ ... real data ... ],
      "total": 36
    }
  }
}

curl → full data visible.
WebUI (Gemma-4 12B via same MCP connection) → tool call panel shows
Input: {} / Output: "No output", and the model reports no data exists.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Connect WebUI to any MCP server whose tools return structuredContent
   with an empty content[] array (e.g. tools implemented against the MCP
   spec's "structured output" schema feature).
2. Trigger a tool call with no required arguments (e.g. a list-type tool).
3. Observe the Connection Log / tool-call detail panel.

### Expected behavior
structuredContent should be read and surfaced to both the UI panel and the
model's context when content is empty, per MCP spec guidance that
structuredContent is a first-class, model-visible field.

### Actual behavior
Only content[] appears to be read. When it's empty, the tool call is
treated as having returned nothing, regardless of structuredContent.

### Additional context
Same failure pattern has been reported against other MCP clients that
predate widespread structuredContent adoption, e.g.
anthropics/claude-code#15412, anthropics/claude-code#55677,

**Summary**
I’m using a llama.cpp OpenAI-compatible server behind ChatWise. Tool calling fails for a simple tool schema that requires one string field and two optional integers. The server/client path reports malformed JSON tool arguments even though the schema is minimal.

**Environment**
- Server: `llama.cpp` OpenAI-compatible HTTP server
- Client: `ChatWise`
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`
- Transport: `/v1/chat/completions`

**Observed behavior**
When the model tries to call a tool like `thread_fetch_messages`, the upstream stack fails with:

```text
Failed to parse tool call arguments as JSON:
[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 1, column 2:
syntax error while parsing object key - unexpected end of input; expected string literal
```

This strongly suggests the generated tool arguments are sometimes just `{` or otherwise truncated before the first key.

**Expected behavior**
For a tool schema like this, the model/tool-call path should emit valid JSON such as:

```json
{"thread_id":"some-id","limit":10}
```

**Minimal schema involved**
This is the actual compact schema shape the server receives for the failing tool:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["thread_id"],
  "properties": {

    "offset": { "type": "integer", "description": "Number of messages to skip (for pagination)" },
    "limit": { "type": "integer", "description": "Maximum number of messages to return (1-100)" },
    "space_id": { "type": "string", "description": "Optional isolation space guard. When provided, the thread must belong to this space." }
  }
}
```

So this is not a complex nested schema, union-heavy schema, or long rich-schema export.

**Reproduction pattern**

- required arg: `thread_id: string`
- optional args:

```

That one was caused by large schema constraints on my side and has been mitigated by switching to compact schemas.

This current issue remains even after schema compaction, so it appears to be a separate failure mode:
- malformed or truncated tool-call JSON arguments
- likely in tool-call generation or streamed argument assembly

**Useful evidence**
- `App` header sent by client: `chatwise`

- failure is specific to JSON argument parsing, not schema compilation

**What would help diagnose**
- raw assistant/tool-call payload before JSON parsing
- whether streamed tool-call argument chunks are being concatenated correctly
- whether llama.cpp function/tool calling has known issues with required string keys in simple object schemas

items.body:
### Name and Version

 # peg-native: tool-call grammar generator emits GBNF that fails its own parser (Kimi K2.7-Code, 22-tool fan-out)

  ### Summary

  When `chat format: peg-native` is selected for the Unsloth `Kimi-K2.7-Code-GGUF` model and the request includes many tools (~22), the grammar generator emits a GBNF
  that immediately fails `parse_grammar` (`E failed to parse grammar`). With no grammar constraint applied, the model then emits a degraded multi-call format the
  parser doesn't recognize, and the call leaks to the client as raw special tokens via `common_chat_peg_parse: unparsed peg-native output: ...`.

  Single tool-call turns work fine. The problem only manifests when the model decides to emit multiple `<|tool_call_begin|>...<|tool_call_end|>` blocks in one
  response.


### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

3xRTX 6000 PRO WS
AMD ThreadRipper PRO 9965WX
320GB DDR5 5600 (8 channel)

### Models

Kimi-K2.7-Code-UD-IQ4_XS

### Problem description & steps to reproduce


  ### Environment

  - **llama.cpp**: `version: 9656 (581e8eca8)` — includes #24329 "chat: harden peg-native tool call parsing"
  - **Model**: [`unsloth/Kimi-K2.7-Code-GGUF`](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Kimi-K2.7-Code-GGUF), quant `UD-IQ4_XS` (12-shard split)
  - **Vision projector**: `mmproj-F16.gguf` from the same repo
  - **Hardware**: 3× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB each), 320 GB ECC RAM
  - **Build flags**: `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="89;90;100"`
  - **Server flags**: `--jinja --chat-template-file <moonshot K2 official template> --reasoning-format deepseek --enable-auto-tool-choice` (full command below)
  - **Auto-detected chat format**: `peg-native`

  The custom chat template is a verbatim port of [Moonshot's official Kimi-K2-Instruct
  template](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct/raw/main/chat_template.jinja). The same bug reproduces with the GGUF-embedded template; mounting the
  official one explicitly was an earlier debug step.

  ### Reproduction

  1. Serve Unsloth `Kimi-K2.7-Code-GGUF` (`UD-IQ4_XS`) with llama-server at commit `581e8eca8`.
  2. Make a chat-completion request that registers ~20+ tools (we hit this via [opencode](https://github.com/opencode-ai/opencode), which exposes a 22-tool surface:
  `Agent`, `AgentSwarm`, `AskUserQuestion`, `Bash`, `CreateGoal`, `CronCreate`, `CronDelete`, `CronList`, `Edit`, `EnterPlanMode`, `ExitPlanMode`, `FetchURL`,
  `GetGoal`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Read`, `Skill`, `TaskList`, `TaskOutput`, `TaskStop`, `TodoList`, `Write`).
  3. Ask the model something that elicits *multiple* tool calls in one response (e.g. "review this PR" — the model wants to call `gh pr view`, `gh pr checks`, `gh pr
  diff`, ...).

  ### Expected

  Either the grammar parses and constrains the model to canonical `functions.NAME:INDEX` format, *or* the post-hoc parser tolerates the degraded variant the model
  emits. Either way the client should receive a valid `tool_calls` JSON array.

  ### Actual

  llama-server logs (trimmed; full grammar omitted for length — happy to attach):

  [grammar generator output begins]
  ...
  tool-Write ::= (("functions." "Write" ":" [0-9]+) "<|tool_call_argument_begin|>") tool-Write-schema "<|tool_call_end|>"?
  tool-Write-schema ::= "{" space tool-Write-schema-path-kv "," space tool-Write-schema-content-kv ( "," space ( tool-Write-schema-mode-kv ) )? "}" space
  tool-Write-schema-content-kv ::= ""content"" space ":" space string
  tool-Write-schema-mode ::= (""overwrite"" | ""append"") space
  tool-Write-schema-mode-kv ::= ""mode"" space ":" space tool-Write-schema-mode
  tool-Write-schema-path-kv ::= ""path"" space ":" space string
  tool-call ::= ("<|tool_call_begin|>" (tool-Agent | tool-AgentSwarm | tool-AskUserQuestion | tool-Bash | tool-CreateGoal | tool-CronCreate | tool-CronDelete |
  tool-CronList | tool-Edit | tool-EnterPlanMode | tool-ExitPlanMode | tool-FetchURL | tool-GetGoal | tool-Glob | tool-Grep | tool-Read | tool-Skill | tool-TaskList |
  tool-TaskOutput | tool-TaskStop | tool-TodoList | tool-Write))* "<|tool_calls_section_end|>"?

  E failed to parse grammar
  I slot launch_slot_: id 0 | task 348 | processing task, is_child = 0
  ...
  I slot      release: id 0 | task 348 | stop processing: n_tokens = 20756, truncated = 0
  W common_chat_peg_parse: unparsed peg-native output: <|tool_call_begin|>functions_Bash_2<|tool_call_argument_begin|>{"command": "gh pr view 2 --json
  number,title,body,author,createdAt,updatedAt,headRefName,baseRefName,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision,comments,reviews", "cwd":
  "/workspace"}<|tool_call_end|><|tool_call_begin|>functions_Bash_3<|tool_call_argument_begin|>{"command": "gh pr checks 2", "cwd":
  "/workspace"}<|tool_call_end|><|tool_call_begin|>functions_Bash_4<|tool_call_argument_begin|>{"command": "git diff --stat main...feature/saas", "cwd":
  "/workspace"}<|tool_call_end|><|tool_calls_section_end|>

  Two distinct problems visible:

  1. **`E failed to parse grammar`** — llama.cpp generates GBNF, then its own `parse_grammar` step rejects it. No grammar constraint is applied to sampling for this
  request.

  2. **Without constraint, the model emits a degraded multi-call format** the post-hoc parser doesn't recognize:
     - Function names use `functions_NAME_INDEX` (underscore-separated) instead of canonical `functions.NAME:INDEX` (dot + colon).
     - The opening `<|tool_calls_section_begin|>` is absent; only the closing `<|tool_calls_section_end|>` is present.
     - Argument JSON includes fields that aren't in the schema (`cwd` in the example above — the Bash tool spec has only `command`).

  The same model on the **same** server emits *canonical* `functions.Bash:0` format when only one tool call is needed per turn — confirmed by a single-tool,
  single-call curl probe returning a clean `tool_calls` array. So this is specifically a many-tools-and-multi-call interaction.

  ### Working single-call response (for contrast)

  Same server, same model, single tool registered, one call requested:

  ```json
  {
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": "",
    "reasoning_content": "We need run bash date and whoami separately. We can make two Bash calls.",
    "tool_calls": [
      {
        "type": "function",
        "function": { "name": "Bash", "arguments": "{\"command\": \"date\"}" },
        "id": "functions.Bash:0"
      }
    ]
  }

  Single-call sampling clearly works end-to-end. The grammar generator path is the only thing that breaks.

  Hypotheses

  I have not isolated the exact GBNF syntax issue, but candidates from inspection of the generated rules:

  - Missing <|tool_calls_section_begin|> literal in the top-level tool-call rule. Canonical Kimi K2 wraps the whole block in
  <|tool_calls_section_begin|>...<|tool_calls_section_end|>; the generator emits only the closing literal.
  - Pipe characters inside double-quoted GBNF strings ("<|tool_call_begin|>"). Standard GBNF treats | as literal inside "..." but parser variants differ.
  - Grammar size — 22 tools × nested schemas produces a large rule set; could be a buffer/recursion-depth issue.

  The whitespace cleanup at a6dff71 (#24624) touches the same files (common/chat-peg-parser.cpp, common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp) but doesn't appear to fix this
  specific case based on inspection of the generated grammar above (no trailing-space artifacts visible).

  Server invocation

  llama-server \
    --model /models/Kimi-K2.7-Code-GGUF/UD-IQ4_XS/Kimi-K2.7-Code-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00012.gguf \
    --mmproj /models/Kimi-K2.7-Code-GGUF/mmproj-F16.gguf \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 \
    --ctx-size 262144 --n-predict 32768 \
    --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
    --ubatch-size 512 -ngl 999 \
    -ot 'blk\.(3[1-9]|[4-5][0-9]|60)\.ffn_.*_exps\.weight=CPU' \
    -ot 'blk\.[0-9]\.=CUDA0' -ot 'blk\.1[0-9]\.=CUDA1' -ot 'blk\.(2[0-9]|30)\.=CUDA2' \
    --threads 32 -mg 0 \
    --jinja --chat-template-file /chat_template.jinja \
    --alias kimi-coder --parallel 1 --no-context-shift \
    --reasoning-format deepseek --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95

items.title: Research: Intel oneAPI Compiler
items.body:
### Research Stage

- [x] Background Research (Let's try to avoid reinventing the wheel)
- [x] Hypothesis Formed (How do you think this will work and it's effect?)
- [x] Strategy / Implementation Forming
- [x] Analysis of results
- [x] Debrief / Documentation (So people in the future can learn from us)

### Previous existing literature and research

The current state of the art, as far as I can tell, would be to use the already defined MSVC based cmake build in the project and pass it a few more optimization flags.

My motivation was to attempt to use the Intel oneAPI compiler (ICX) instead of MSVC for an even more hyper-optimized build for my system. Currently, it's not as directly supported as simply using a cmake target. In fact, in the Python code I'll post below, I had to force and work around a ton of stuff.

### Hypothesis

Well, I thought I could get it to work somehow. Especially if I iterated and meta-prompted a few AIs a bit. 🤣

### Implementation

My Python build script is below:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

"""
llama.cpp Build Script for Intel ICX and NVIDIA CUDA

Author: 
Steven Bock

Utilizing:
Google Gemini 2.5 Pro,
ChatGPT 5, 
and Qwen3 Coder A3B 30b (Unsloth Build)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
This script automates the build process for llama.cpp on Windows using the
Intel oneAPI (ICX) and NVIDIA CUDA compilers.

It generates a dedicated CMake toolchain file to ensure a consistent, reliable,
and complete build environment. This approach is superior to manually setting
environment variables or CMake command-line arguments because it centralizes
all build-critical definitions in one place, preventing conflicts and ensuring
that CMake does not fall back on potentially incorrect auto-detected settings.

This version includes:
-   Full support for both 'Release' and 'Debug' build types.
-   Explicit control over CPU architecture flags for portability.
-   Direct MKL library linking to bypass CMake's potentially fragile FindBLAS module.
-   Full MSVC toolchain compatibility for the Intel compiler via the `-Qmsvc-target` flag.
-   Optional suppression of all compiler warnings for a cleaner build log.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1.  Configure the settings in the `CONFIG` dictionary below. You must provide the
    correct paths to your llama.cpp project and vcpkg installation.
2.  Run this script from an initialized Intel oneAPI Command Prompt. This is crucial
    as it sets up the necessary environment variables (like PATH and MKLROOT)
    for the Intel and NVIDIA compilers and libraries.
    (e.g., from the Start Menu, find and run "Intel oneAPI Command Prompt for...").
3.  To see compiler warnings, which can be useful for debugging, run the script
    with the --warn flag:
    python llamacpp_build.py --warn
"""

# --- Standard Library Imports ---
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

# --- Third-Party / Windows-Specific Imports ---
import ctypes
from ctypes import wintypes
import argparse

# --- Primary Configuration ---
# All user-configurable settings are centralized here for ease of use.
CONFIG = {
    # Path to the root of your local llama.cpp repository.
    "project_dir": Path("D:/Code/llama.cpp"),
    # Path to the root of your vcpkg installation.
    # This is used to locate the vcpkg.cmake toolchain file.
    "vcpkg_root_path": Path("C:/vcpkg"),
    # Number of parallel jobs to use for compilation.
    # Defaults to the number of CPU cores, or 8 if detection fails.
    "build_jobs": os.cpu_count() or 8,
    # NVIDIA CUDA architecture to target. This should match your GPU.
    # Examples: RTX 30 series -> 8.6 -> 86; RTX 40 series -> 8.9 -> 89.
    # Find yours here: https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus
    "cuda_arch": 86,
    # The build type. Can be "Release" for an optimized build or "Debug"
    # for a build with debugging symbols.
    "build_type": "Release",
}

def generate_cmake_toolchain_file(
    build_dir: Path, mkl_root: Path, cpu_arch: str, extra_host_flags: str, extra_cuda_flags: str
) -> Path:
    """
    Generates a complete CMake toolchain file.

    This file is the heart of the stable build process. It explicitly tells
    CMake which compilers, linkers, and libraries to use, preventing it from
    auto-detecting and possibly choosing the wrong tools or paths.

    Args:
        build_dir: The directory where the toolchain file will be saved.
        mkl_root: The root path of the Intel MKL installation.
        cpu_arch: The target CPU architecture (e.g., "AMD64").
        extra_host_flags: Additional flags for the C/C++ host compiler (icx).
        extra_cuda_flags: Additional flags for the CUDA compiler (nvcc).

    Returns:
        The path to the newly created toolchain file.
    """
    # Define the full path for the toolchain file.
    toolchain_path = build_dir / "intel_cuda_toolchain.cmake"
    # Define the full path to the vcpkg toolchain, which handles dependency management.
    vcpkg_tc_path = (CONFIG["vcpkg_root_path"] / "scripts" / "buildsystems" / "vcpkg.cmake").as_posix()

    # Get the 8.3 short path names for MKL paths. This is a critical compatibility
    # fix for some versions of the Intel compiler or other build tools that may
    # struggle with long paths or paths containing spaces.
    mkl_include_path_short = Path(get_short_path_name(str(mkl_root / "include")))
    mkl_lib_path_short = Path(get_short_path_name(str(mkl_root / "lib")))

    # Define the exact MKL libraries to link against. This bypasses CMake's
    # FindBLAS module entirely, providing a more reliable link process.
    mkl_libs = ";".join([
        f"{mkl_lib_path_short.as_posix()}/mkl_intel_lp64_dll.lib",
        f"{mkl_lib_path_short.as_posix()}/mkl_intel_thread_dll.lib",
        f"{mkl_lib_path_short.as_posix()}/mkl_core_dll.lib",
    ])

    print(f"--> Forcing MKL include path to: {mkl_include_path_short}")
    print(f"--> Forcing MKL library path to: {mkl_lib_path_short}")

    # Use textwrap.dedent for a clean, readable multiline string.
    content = textwrap.dedent(f'''
        # CMake Toolchain File for Intel ICX + NVIDIA CUDA (Stable Version)
        # Generated by llamacpp_build.py. This file is self-contained and authoritative.

        # Include the vcpkg toolchain file first. This allows vcpkg to manage all
        # other third-party libraries required by llama.cpp.
        include("{vcpkg_tc_path}")

        # --- System & Compiler Definition ---
        # Define the target system.
        set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME Windows)
        set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR "{cpu_arch}" CACHE STRING "System Processor" FORCE)
        # Explicitly tell CMake we are not cross-compiling.
        set(CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING FALSE CACHE BOOL "Force disable cross-compiling")

        # Explicitly set the C and C++ compilers to Intel's ICX and the linker to MSVC's link.exe.
        set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER icx.exe)
        set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER icx.exe)
        set(CMAKE_LINKER link.exe)
        
        # --- Linker & Runtime Library Settings ---
        # Force the use of the Multithreaded DLL runtime library (/MD or /MDd).
        # This ensures consistency across all compiled units and dependencies.
        set(CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY "MultiThreadedDLL" CACHE STRING "" FORCE)

        # --- Compatibility Fixes ---
        # Force a consistent namespace for the nlohmann::json library. This prevents
        # ODR (One Definition Rule) violations if different parts of the project
        # are compiled with different settings for this library.
        add_compile_definitions(NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE=json_abi_v3_11_3)

        # --- Compiler Flags (with compatibility fixes) ---
        # Set the INITIAL flags for both C and CXX. These are applied to all build types.
        # -Qmsvc-target: This crucial flag tells icx to behave like MSVC, ensuring ABI compatibility.
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS_INIT   "-Qmsvc-target {extra_host_flags} /DNLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE=json_abi_v3_11_3" CACHE STRING "" FORCE)
        set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_INIT "-Qmsvc-target {extra_host_flags} /DNLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE=json_abi_v3_11_3" CACHE STRING "" FORCE)

        # Define specific flags for Release and Debug builds.
        # Release: /O3 (heavy optimization), /Ob2 (inline expansion), /DNDEBUG (disables asserts), /MD, /fp:fast (fast floating point).
        # Debug: /Od (no optimization), /Zi (debug info), /DDEBUG, /MDd, /EHsc (exception handling).
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELEASE   "/O3 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG /MD /fp:fast" CACHE STRING "C Release Flags" FORCE)
        set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE "/O3 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG /MD /EHsc /fp:fast" CACHE STRING "CXX Release Flags" FORCE)
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS_DEBUG     "/Od /Zi /DDEBUG /MDd" CACHE STRING "C Debug Flags" FORCE)
        set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG   "/Od /Zi /DDEBUG /MDd /EHsc" CACHE STRING "CXX Debug Flags" FORCE)

        # Define all CUDA-specific flags for maximum stability and performance.
        set(CMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS "--use_fast_math -Xptxas --allow-expensive-optimizations=true,-O3 {extra_cuda_flags}" CACHE STRING "CUDA Compiler Flags" FORCE)

        # --- BLAS/MKL Override ---
        # Force all BLAS-related variables to our specific MKL paths and libraries.
        # This completely bypasses CMake's FindBLAS.cmake module, which can be unreliable.
        set(BLA_VENDOR Intel10_64lp CACHE STRING "BLAS Vendor" FORCE)
        set(BLAS_INCLUDE_DIRS "{mkl_include_path_short.as_posix()}" CACHE PATH "BLAS Include Directory" FORCE)
        set(BLAS_LIBRARIES "{mkl_libs}" CACHE STRING "BLAS Libraries" FORCE)
        # Also set the GGML-specific BLAS variables for good measure.
        set(GGML_BLAS_INCLUDE_DIRS "{mkl_include_path_short.as_posix()}" CACHE PATH "GGML BLAS Include Directory" FORCE)
        set(GGML_BLAS_LIBRARIES "{mkl_libs}" CACHE STRING "GGML BLAS Libraries" FORCE)
    ''')
    try:
        # Create the build directory if it doesn't exist.
        build_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        # Write the generated content to the toolchain file.
        toolchain_path.write_text(content)
        print(f"--> CMake toolchain file generated at: {toolchain_path}")
        return toolchain_path
    except IOError as e:
        # Handle potential file writing errors.
        print(f"\nFATAL: Could not write toolchain file: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

def run_command(command: list, cwd: Path, env: dict | None = None) -> None:
    """
    Executes a subprocess command and handles errors.

    Args:
        command: A list of strings representing the command and its arguments.
        cwd: The working directory from which to run the command.
        env: An optional dictionary of environment variables.
    """
    # Convert all command parts to strings for subprocess.
    str_command = [str(c) for c in command]
    print(f"--> Executing: {' '.join(str_command)}")
    try:
        # Run the command. check=True will raise CalledProcessError on non-zero exit codes.
        # capture_output=False streams the output directly to the console.
        subprocess.run(str_command, cwd=cwd, check=True, text=True, capture_output=False, env=env)
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
        # If the command fails, print an error and exit the script.
        print(f"\nFATAL: Command failed with exit code {e.returncode}.", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

def get_short_path_name(long_name: str) -> str:
    """
    Gets the 8.3 short path name for a given long path using the Windows API.
    This is a compatibility fix for the Intel compiler.

    Args:
        long_name: The long path string to convert.

    Returns:
        The 8.3 short path, or the original path if conversion fails.
    """
    # Define the buffer size for the output path.
    output_buf_size = 260
    # Create a buffer to hold the result.
    output_buf = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(output_buf_size)
    # Call the Win32 API function 'GetShortPathNameW' ('W' for wide/Unicode characters).
    needs_conversion = ctypes.windll.kernel32.GetShortPathNameW(wintypes.LPCWSTR(long_name), output_buf, output_buf_size)
    # If the function returns a length greater than 0, the conversion was successful.
    return output_buf.value if needs_conversion > 0 else long_name

    """Main function to orchestrate the entire build process."""
    # --- Argument Parsing ---

items.title: Feature Request: server-tools: secure shell commands
items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

1. Discuss current security issues with the `exec_shell_command` tool. 
2. Propose to add a new `exec_command` tool which does not call a shell but directly send commands in a fixed syntax form, still allowing placeholders from the context, but preventing by construction any shell interpolation.
3. Feed this tool with commands read from a specification file.

This enhancement ticket follows a suggestion from @ngxson regarding `--tools` in #24659. 
I've launched as well a discussion on the same subject, https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/24841. Currently, this discussion seems to point out that I'm not alone to identify a need for a better security mechanism in the shell-type tool.

### Motivation

I bet that many users of llama.cpp start with the tools enabled (this is my case) including the shell execution. With great power comes great responsibility, sure, but there is currently no safe alternative in llama.cpp to allow shell commands AND control the way these commands affect the underlying system.

The `exec_shell_command` allows execution of any kind of command, and it implies the shell interpolation. 

Currently, the `exec_shell_command` (in `tools/server/server-tools.cpp`) for a given `command` requests execution (to `io->run`) of the argument list e.g. `{"sh", "-c", command}` ("cmd" on Windows). This is the issue. The `command` is sent as a single string to the shell, which then implies interpolation. Any syntax is allowed. By allowing the `--tools exec_shell_command` (included in `--tools all`) we give the LLM full access to any command.

The `exec_shell_command` must be kept for systems where e.g. the LLM can work in a perfectly sealed container. Other LLM engine implementations also provide this 'bash' tool. The SKILLS definition at https://agentskills.io/specification#allowed-tools-field can restrict the shell to a subset of commands such as Bash(git:*), but this in no way avoids arbitrary commands which would follow the initial word match. I personally doubt this can remain safe in production. 

I do not want to take such a risk in production servers, and thus need a finer grain mechanism to control which commands are allowed, in a secured way. Still I do not want to implement each tool in the `server-tools.cpp`. 

A filter based on forbidden characters (e.g. no `!|><;` ...) and commands (no `sudo` and other nice pitfalls) is not a good solution either. There are many ways to bypass, and this would certainly be a never ending story. 

### Possible Implementation

I suggest two items.

**Command execution**: How to avoid shell interpolation and command injection.

I suggest to add a new tool which avoids the shell interpolation, and sends the `command` above as a fixed set of parts, all of them being sent as static strings. This prevents by construction shell interpolation. There is no shell. The command could be described as a static string in a specification (see below) containing placeholders which allow replacement by the LLM. 

For instance, if you wish to allow listing of a directory, you would provide something like `ls {directory}`. This is then split into a vector of strings {`ls`,`{directory}`}. Then the placeholders are replaced from the tool call context, but arguments remain single strings in a fixed length list.

The `exec_shell_command` can be specified within this frame as a command `sh -c {command}` (which brings shell interpolation).

I have implemented this in `tools/server/server-tools.cpp` as `exec_command` tool in my fork https://github.com/farhi/llama.cpp/tree/master

Once we have this, comes the question how to define such tools ?

**Commands specification**: How to define a list of allowed command sets

We thus seek for a way to specify tools without actually implementing each of them. 
Most tools are defined as JSON schema, and this is the case with currently implemented ones in llama-server. 
A shell-type command tool requires something like:
```
            {"function", {
                {"name", name},
                {"description", "Execute a shell command and return its output (stdout and stderr combined)."},
                {"parameters", {
                    {"type", "object"},
                    {"properties", {
                        {"command",         {{"type", "string"},  {"description", "Shell command to execute"}}},
                    {"required", json::array({"command"})},
                }},
            }},
```
In my view, what is important here is the "name", the "description", and the "command".

A specification in a file seems logic, as we want to pass-on information to the server at start.
The format of such file(s) can be anything as long as it provides the required information. Multiple entries per file should be allowed, and multiple files as well.
I tend to prefer file formats which can easily be read by humans.

I have chosen a JSON object array such as:
```
[
  {
    "name": "get_ip",
    "description": "Get the public IP address of the server",
    "command": "curl ifconfig.me"
  },
  {
    "name": "list_files",
    "description": "List all files in a directory",
    "command": "ls -la {directory}"
  },
  {
    "name": "date_now",
    "description": "Get the current time",
    "command": "date"
  }
]
```

Last, I suggest to provide such files as argument to `--tools`, and parse them when initializing the `server_tools::setup`.

I attach the `server-tools.cpp` file which implements most of this stuff (with JSON command specifications). The modified part is at the end of the `server-tools.cpp` file after the other tools, just before the public API. It consists in `tokenize_command`, `server_tool_exec_command`, `parse_json_tools` as well as a slight modification in `server_tools::setup` to read `--tools` argument files.
In my fork, I have also adapted the `server-tools.h`, `common/args.cpp` and `tools/server/README.md`.

items.body:
### Name and Version

$ ./llama-server --version
ggml_cuda_init: found 2 CUDA devices (Total VRAM: 97020 MiB):
  Device 0: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, compute capability 8.9, VMM: yes, VRAM: 48510 MiB

version: 8882 (ca7f7b7b9)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --n-gpu-layers 99 --ctx-size 260000 --seed 3407 --model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf --split-mode layer --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 --flash-attn on --metrics --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --jinja --swa-full
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce


## Problem Description

When  Claude Code use it's built-in `TaskUpdate` tool with llama.cpp as the inference engine, the tool call validation fails incorrectly for `anyOf` schema types.

The `TaskUpdate` tool is a built-in tool provided by Claude Code itself (not a custom tool), used for updating task status in the task management system.

## Schema Definition

The `TaskUpdate` tool's `status` parameter is defined as:

```json
{
  "name": "TaskUpdate",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "taskId": {
        "description": "The ID of the task to update",
        "type": "string"
      },
      "status": {
        "anyOf": [
          {
            "type": "string",
            "enum": ["pending", "in_progress", "completed"]
          },
          {
            "type": "string",
            "const": "deleted"
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    "required": ["taskId", "status"]
  }
}
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use Claude Code CLI with llama.cpp as the inference engine
2. Ask Claude to update a task status (e.g., "mark task 1 as in progress")
3. Claude attempts to call the `TaskUpdate` tool with `status: "in_progress"`
4. The tool call fails with a validation error

**Note**: The error appears in Claude Code's output when the tool call validation fails.

## Error Message

```json
{
  "code": "invalid_union",
  "errors": [
    [
      {
        "code": "invalid_value",
        "values": ["pending", "in_progress", "completed"],
        "path": [],
        "message": "Invalid option: expected one of \"pending\"|\"in_progress\"|\"completed\""
      }
    ],
    [
      {
        "code": "invalid_value",
        "values": ["deleted"],
        "path": [],
        "message": "Invalid input: expected \"deleted\""
      }
    ]
  ],
  "path": ["status"],
  "message": "Invalid input"
}
```

## Root Cause Analysis

This issue was identified by **examining the Claude Code source code**. The validation error originates from the tool call processing logic in Claude Code.

The error message is confusing because:

1. The user (Claude) is passing a valid enum value (`in_progress`) from the first `anyOf` branch
2. The error shows BOTH branches failed validation, including the second branch showing `expected "deleted"`
3. **Based on the source code analysis**, the actual root cause appears to be that the string value is being passed **with literal quote characters included** (i.e., the value is `"\"in_progress\""`) rather than just `in_progress`

The source code reveals that when the model outputs a tool call with string parameters, the JSON string delimiters (quotes) may be incorrectly included as part of the value itself during parsing.

## Expected Behavior

1. **If the value is valid**: The tool call should succeed when passing a valid enum value from any `anyOf` branch
2. **If the value is invalid**: The error message should clearly indicate:
   - What value was actually received
   - Which specific branch failed and why
   - The difference between the received value and expected values

## Request

Please investigate:
1. How tool call arguments are parsed and validated for `anyOf` schema types in llama.cpp
2. Whether string values are being correctly extracted from JSON (removing delimiters)
3. Whether the validation error message clearly shows the actual received value

This issue affects the usability of Claude Code's built-in tools when using llama.cpp as the inference engine
